checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Are all three sidecar verification layers (structural, KZG, Merkle) enforced before acceptance?

reachability.notes: Attacker attempts to inject tampered data columns via gossip.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify all code paths where data column sidecars enter the node from gossip (e.g., lighthouse: beacon_node/beacon_chain/src/data_column_verification.rs, prysm: beacon-chain/core/peerdas/p2p_interface.go, erigon: cl/phase1/network/services/data_column_sidecar_service.go, lodestar: packages/beacon-node/src/chain/validation/dataColumnSidecar.ts, nimbus: beacon_chain/spec/peerdas_helpers.nim). 2. Verify that verify_data_column_sidecar (structural), verify_data_column_sidecar_kzg_proofs (cryptographic), and verify_data_column_sidecar_inclusion_proof (Merkle) are ALL invoked before any sidecar is accepted. 3. Construct a sidecar that passes structural checks but has an invalid KZG proof - verify it is rejected. 4. Construct a sidecar that passes structural and KZG checks but has an invalid Merkle inclusion proof - verify it is rejected. 5. Verify there is no code path that short-circuits acceptance after only one or two verification layers. 6. Check that each verification function returns an error (not a silent pass) on invalid input.
executable_checks: Fuzz test data column sidecar parsing with random bytes to verify structural validation catches malformed sidecars
Unit test: sidecar with valid structure but tampered cell commitments must fail KZG verification
Unit test: sidecar with valid KZG proofs but tampered Merkle branch must fail inclusion proof verification
Integration test: ensure all three layers are called in sequence and no early acceptance occurs
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0046, Trust Boundary: tb-001, Threat: tb-001-Tampering. Bypassing any single layer enables injection of invalid data, undermining PeerDAS data availability guarantees.

checklist.title: Verify Node Behavior: Does the beacon node correctly reject sidecars with individually tampered verification layers?

reachability.notes: Attacker attempts to inject tampered data columns via gossip.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. For each verification layer independently, craft a sidecar that passes all OTHER layers but fails THIS specific layer. 2. Submit each crafted sidecar via gossip and verify the beacon node rejects it with the correct error code. 3. Verify that REJECT (not IGNORE) is returned for cryptographic failures, as per spec requirements. 4. Check that the peer scoring system penalizes the sender appropriately for submitting invalid sidecars.
executable_checks: Unit test: tampered structure (wrong column index) causes REJECT, not IGNORE
Unit test: valid structure but invalid KZG proof causes REJECT
Unit test: valid structure and KZG but invalid Merkle proof causes REJECT
Verify peer scoring deducts reputation for invalid sidecar submissions
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0046, Supporting node check for actor-beacon-node and actor-gossip-network.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is gossip validation ordered from cheapest to most expensive checks to prevent DoS amplification?

reachability.notes: Attacker floods gossip with invalid sidecars to waste CPU on expensive checks.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the data column sidecar gossip validation function in each client implementation. 2. Trace the exact order of validation steps: (a) structural checks (column index bounds, field sizes), (b) subnet validation, (c) slot timing checks, (d) signature verification, (e) parent/ancestry checks, (f) KZG proof verification, (g) Merkle inclusion proof verification. 3. Verify that cheap operations (structural, subnet) precede expensive operations (KZG, Merkle). 4. Construct a sidecar that fails the cheapest check (e.g., invalid column index) and measure CPU time consumed before rejection - it should be negligible. 5. Construct a sidecar that fails signature verification and verify KZG proofs are NOT computed before the signature failure is detected. 6. Profile the cost of each validation step to confirm ordering is monotonically increasing in expense.
executable_checks: Benchmark test: measure time to reject sidecar with invalid structure vs invalid KZG proof
Stress test: flood node with sidecars failing at cheapest check - verify CPU usage remains bounded
Code audit: verify no early KZG computation before cheaper checks in the validation pipeline
Static analysis: trace validation function call order and confirm monotonic cost increase
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0047, Trust Boundary: tb-001, Threat: tb-001-DoS. Misordered checks amplify DoS by forcing expensive cryptographic operations on invalid messages.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Can a non-proposer node get a sidecar accepted by setting proposer_index to a scheduled proposer?

reachability.notes: Attacker attempts privilege escalation by claiming to be a scheduled proposer.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the sidecar validation logic that checks proposer_index against the expected proposer schedule. 2. Verify that signature verification occurs BEFORE proposer_index is used for any trust-relevant decision. 3. Craft a sidecar where proposer_index is set to a legitimate scheduled proposer but signed with an attacker's key - verify it is rejected due to signature mismatch. 4. Craft a sidecar where proposer_index is set to a legitimate scheduled proposer AND the signature is valid for the attacker's key (not the proposer's) - verify it is rejected because the signature key does not match the expected proposer. 5. Verify that the proposer schedule lookup (get_beacon_proposer_index) uses the correct state and slot. 6. Check for TOCTOU between signature verification and proposer schedule lookup. 7. Ensure the validation enforces that block.proposer_index matches the sidecar.signed_beacon_block_header.message.proposer_index.
executable_checks: Unit test: sidecar with spoofed proposer_index but wrong signature key is rejected
Unit test: sidecar with valid proposer_index but signed by non-proposer validator is rejected
Integration test: submit sidecar impersonating a scheduled proposer and verify rejection
Verify no code path accepts proposer_index without verifying corresponding signature
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0048, Trust Boundary: tb-001, Threat: tb-001-EoP. Accepting unauthorized proposer would allow injecting arbitrary data into the data availability layer.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does p256verify revert on any input besides out-of-gas?

reachability.notes: Attacker submits transaction invoking p256verify with crafted inputs via P2P.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the p256verify precompile implementation in each execution client (e.g., foundry: crates/evm/core/src/precompiles.rs, besu: CHANGELOG.md references, ethereumjs: packages/evm/examples/precompiles/100-p256verify.ts). 2. Test with invalid inputs: (a) empty input, (b) input shorter than 160 bytes, (c) input longer than 160 bytes, (d) r=0, (e) s=0, (f) point not on curve, (g) point at infinity, (h) r >= n, (i) s >= n. 3. For each invalid input, verify the precompile returns empty bytes (0 bytes output) rather than reverting. 4. Verify that the ONLY condition under which the precompile reverts is out-of-gas (insufficient gas supplied). 5. Test across multiple client implementations and verify behavior is identical for all edge-case inputs. 6. Check that gas cost is charged consistently regardless of input validity (gas is consumed even for invalid inputs returning empty bytes).
executable_checks: Differential fuzz test: compare p256verify behavior across all EL clients for random inputs
Unit test: every category of invalid input returns empty bytes, not revert
Unit test: out-of-gas is the only condition that produces a revert
Gas accounting test: verify gas is consumed correctly for both valid and invalid inputs
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0049, Trust Boundary: tb-001, Threat: tb-001-Tampering. Based on EIP-7951. Unexpected revert could cause consensus split between clients.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is p256verify input validation performed in the exact specified sequential order across all clients?

reachability.notes: Different validation orderings between clients cause consensus splits for edge-case inputs.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. For each EL client implementation, trace the p256verify validation logic and document the exact order of checks. 2. Verify the order matches: (1) length check (160 bytes), (2) r in [1, n-1], (3) s in [1, n-1], (4) qx in [0, p-1], (5) qy in [0, p-1], (6) curve equation check (qy^2 = qx^3 + ax + b mod p), (7) infinity check. 3. Craft inputs that fail at each specific step and verify all clients return the same result (empty bytes). 4. Craft edge-case inputs where validation order matters: (a) input that would pass step 6 but fail step 2 - verify it fails at step 2, not step 6; (b) r=0 with a valid-looking point - verify it fails at step 2. 5. Test the boundary between steps: craft an input where r=n (fails step 2) but also has qy off-curve (fails step 6) - verify all clients fail at step 2. 6. Cross-client differential testing: run identical edge-case inputs through all clients and verify identical outputs.
executable_checks: Differential test: craft input failing at each validation step, verify same behavior across all EL clients
Unit test: input with r=0 fails at step 2 before reaching curve check at step 6
Unit test: input with valid r,s but off-curve point fails at step 6 (not earlier)
Boundary test: input at exact boundary values (r=n, s=n, qx=p, qy=p) verified across clients
Static analysis: trace validation order in each client implementation and compare against spec
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0050, Trust Boundaries: tb-001, tb-003, Threat: tb-001-Tampering. Validation order divergence is the primary consensus-split vector for EIP-7951.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is the point-at-infinity check on R' mandatory during p256verify signature verification?

reachability.notes: Missing infinity check is a known RIP-7212 vulnerability fix.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the p256 signature verification algorithm implementation in each EL client. 2. Locate the step where R' = u1*G + u2*Q is computed. 3. Verify that an explicit check for R' == point-at-infinity is performed BEFORE extracting the x-coordinate. 4. Craft a signature where the computed R' would be the point at infinity (this requires specific (r, s, Q) combinations). 5. Submit this crafted signature via a transaction calling p256verify and verify the precompile returns 0 (failure), not 1 (success). 6. Verify that the infinity check is not silently handled by the underlying crypto library in a platform-dependent way. 7. Test across multiple clients to ensure deterministic behavior for infinity-result inputs. 8. Review the RIP-7212 vulnerability disclosure and confirm the fix is applied.

code_locations.function: p256verify ECDSA verification step: R' infinity check

executable_checks: Unit test: signature producing R' = infinity returns 0 (not 1 or revert)
Differential test: compare infinity-edge-case behavior across all EL client implementations
Code audit: verify explicit infinity check exists and is not delegated to library-dependent behavior
Regression test: verify RIP-7212 vulnerability fix is applied in all client implementations
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0051, Trust Boundary: tb-003, Threat: tb-003-EoP. This is a KNOWN vulnerability from RIP-7212. Missing infinity check allows forged signatures to pass verification, enabling unauthorized actions in P256-secured smart contracts.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does p256verify use modular reduction (r' == r mod n) rather than direct equality for signature comparison?

reachability.notes: Known RIP-7212 vulnerability fix. Direct comparison causes consensus splits.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the final comparison step in the p256 ECDSA verification algorithm in each EL client. 2. Verify that the comparison uses modular reduction: r' = x-coordinate(R') mod n, then check r' == r. 3. Craft a test case with an x-coordinate of R' that exceeds the subgroup order n (x >= n, which is possible since p > n for P-256). 4. Submit two transactions: one where direct comparison would succeed but modular would fail, and vice versa. 5. Verify all clients produce the same result using modular comparison. 6. Specifically test x-coordinates in the range [n, p-1] where x mod n != x. 7. Cross-client differential testing: run identical edge-case inputs through geth, besu, nethermind, erigon, and reth.
executable_checks: Unit test: signature with R' x-coordinate in [n, p-1] verifies correctly with modular reduction
Differential test: compare direct equality vs modular reduction for edge-case x-coordinates across clients
Code audit: verify all clients use mod n reduction, not direct comparison
Construct concrete test vector with x > n and verify cross-client consensus
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0052, Trust Boundary: tb-003, Threat: tb-003-EoP. Known RIP-7212 vulnerability fix. The P-256 curve has p > n by ~2^128, so there exist valid R' points with x >= n. Non-modular comparison causes consensus split.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is the gas cap GAS_CAP=16777216 (2^24) enforced at both txpool admission and block validation?

reachability.notes: Attacker submits transaction with gasLimit > 2^24 via P2P or private channels.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the txpool admission logic in each EL client and locate where gasLimit is validated against the cap. 2. Identify the block validation logic and locate where per-transaction gasLimit is validated. 3. Submit a transaction with gasLimit = 16777217 (2^24 + 1) via RPC/P2P and verify it is rejected at txpool admission. 4. Construct a block containing a transaction with gasLimit = 16777217 and submit via P2P - verify the block is rejected at block validation. 5. Test boundary values: gasLimit = 16777216 (should pass), gasLimit = 16777217 (should fail). 6. Verify that both layers use strict comparison (>) not (>=) against the cap value. 7. Test that private transaction submission channels (e.g., Flashbots, PBS builders) also enforce the cap. 8. Verify that the cap applies regardless of transaction type (legacy, EIP-1559, EIP-4844, EIP-7702).
executable_checks: Unit test: transaction with gasLimit > 2^24 rejected at txpool
Unit test: block containing transaction with gasLimit > 2^24 rejected at validation
Boundary test: gasLimit = 2^24 accepted, gasLimit = 2^24 + 1 rejected at both layers
Test all transaction types (legacy, 1559, 4844, 7702) against the cap
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0053, Trust Boundaries: tb-001, tb-003, Threat: tb-001-Tampering. Based on EIP-7825. Bypassing gas cap allows single transaction to consume excessive block resources.

checklist.title: Verify Node Behavior: Do txpool and block validator both enforce the gas cap for all transaction submission channels?

reachability.notes: Attacker submits transaction with gasLimit > 2^24 via P2P or private channels.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Enumerate all transaction submission channels: eth_sendRawTransaction RPC, P2P transaction propagation, engine_newPayloadV* from CL, builder block submissions. 2. For each channel, submit a transaction with gasLimit exceeding 2^24 and verify rejection. 3. Specifically test engine_newPayloadV* with a block containing an oversized transaction - verify the EL rejects it. 4. Test that the cap is enforced even when the block's total gas usage is within the block gas limit.
checklist.bug_class: Resource Exhaustion / Bypass via Alternative Channel

code_locations.function: Transaction gas cap - all entry points

executable_checks: Integration test: submit oversized transaction via each entry point and verify rejection
Test engine_newPayloadV* with block containing oversized transaction
Verify cap enforcement is independent of block gas limit
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0053, Supporting node check for actor-tx-submitter, actor-txpool, actor-block-validator.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does block validation check ALL transactions for gas cap compliance without early-exit optimization?

reachability.notes: Malicious builder places oversized transaction at end of block to exploit early-exit optimizations.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the block validation function that iterates over transactions and checks gas limits. 2. Code audit: verify there is no early-exit optimization that stops checking after (a) cumulative gas exceeds block limit, (b) first N transactions pass, (c) any other condition. 3. Construct a block with 100 valid transactions followed by 1 transaction with gasLimit > 2^24 at the end - verify the entire block is rejected. 4. Construct a block where the oversized transaction is at position 0, middle, and last - verify rejection in all cases. 5. Test with a block where cumulative gas of valid transactions already exceeds block gas limit AND the last transaction exceeds the per-transaction cap - verify the per-transaction cap violation is still detected. 6. Verify that the error message identifies the specific transaction that violated the cap.
executable_checks: Unit test: block with oversized transaction at position 0 is rejected
Unit test: block with oversized transaction at last position is rejected
Unit test: block with oversized transaction at middle position is rejected
Code audit: verify no early-exit in the transaction validation loop
Test block where cumulative gas already exceeds block limit but per-tx cap violation exists at end
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0054, Trust Boundary: tb-003, Threat: tb-003-Tampering. A malicious builder could exploit early-exit optimization to sneak oversized transactions into blocks.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is the gas cap value (16777216) identical at both txpool and block validation layers?

reachability.notes: Divergent constants could be caused by implementation bug in one layer.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. In each EL client, locate the constant or variable defining the gas cap for txpool validation. 2. Locate the constant or variable defining the gas cap for block validation. 3. Verify they reference the same constant (ideally a single source of truth) or have identical values. 4. Search for any conditional logic that could cause different effective cap values (e.g., feature flags, fork-dependent values). 5. Craft a transaction with gasLimit = 16777216 (exactly at cap) and verify it passes both layers identically. 6. Code audit: verify there is no off-by-one between the two enforcement points (e.g., one uses > and the other uses >=). 7. Check if the constant is hardcoded or configurable - if configurable, verify both layers read from the same config.
executable_checks: Static analysis: verify both enforcement points reference the same constant or identical values
Unit test: transaction at exact cap boundary (16777216) passes both layers
Code audit: verify no off-by-one between > and >= comparisons at the two layers
Verify single source of truth for the gas cap constant in each client
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0055, Trust Boundaries: tb-001, tb-003. CONDITIONAL SCOPE: This property requires further investigation as it depends on implementation bugs rather than external attacks. Different gas cap values between layers would cause blocks to be built with transactions that are then rejected, or vice versa.
